title: August 10, 2026: Death toll rises to 132 following 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia | CNN
text:
Please see here for the latest updates.

• Growing death toll: At least 132 people died and 570 injured as a result of the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck in western Colombia, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities. You can track developments here, in maps and charts.

• Rescue efforts: Emergency responders are racing to dig people out of the rubble. Among the collapsed structures were the pediatric and neonatal sections of a hospital in Cali. The government has declared a national disaster and deployed soldiers to the area.

• Where it happened: The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in an underdeveloped area of western Colombia, about 150 miles west of Bogotá. The tremor was felt strongly in the nation’s capital, with alarms sounding and people evacuating to the streets as a precaution.

At least 85 people have died in the Colombian city of Cali following the earthquake, the city’s mayor Alejandro Eder said in an update posted to X early Tuesday.

In an earlier update, Eder said 188 people were still missing in the city, while 37 had been rescued.

Some 40 buildings have collapsed in the cultural hub of about 2 million people in Colombia’s southwest, known for salsa dancing.

Among the damaged infrastructure was a hospital where several patients were trapped under the rubble of collapsed parts of the hospital, including the pediatrics department, according to the local governor.

Eder said Monday about 600 troops had been deployed to assist the response, with another 4-500 expected overnight and an additional 232 requested.

A curfew was put in place from 8 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday local time to protect residents while rescue operations continue.

Emergency response efforts are ongoing after a powerful earthquake struck Colombia Monday morning, collapsing buildings and sending people across the country racing out of their homes, workplaces and schools.

At least 132 have died and 570 have been injured as a result of the magnitude 7.4 quake, including 60 deaths in the western city of Pereira alone, according to an update from the Colombian Association of Capital Cities Monday evening. These figures are likely to rise as rescue operations continue.

Here are the latest headlines on the earthquake and the emergency response:

Michael Rios, Rocio Munoz, Fernando Ramos and Jennifer Hansler contributed reporting.

Videos geolocated by CNN shows the moments several buildings in the Colombian city of Pereira collapsed during the deadly 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the South American nation on Monday.

In Pereira, the municipality which has recorded the highest number of fatalities, social media footage showed the moment a building collapsed and engulfed onlookers with dust and debris in the city’s Bolivar Plaza.

Another video geolocated by CNN shows people running for cover as another building collapses in Pereira.

At least 60 people have died in Pereira alone according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, which earlier took part in an disaster response meeting with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

Much of the damage from Monday’s earthquake has been concentrated in a mountainous, lush and culturally important region which helps to power Colombia’s economy and draws hundreds of thousands of tourists annually.

Colombia’s so-called coffee axis, or Eje Cafetero, is a major coffee-growing area in the center of the country, known for its green, steep sided-valleys dotted with coffee plantations. Recognized by UNESCO for its unique cultural heritage and sustainable farming traditions, the area encompasses the cities of Manizales, Pereira, Amenia and Ibagué.

Coffee is one of Colombia’s largest exports and a significant part of the country’s cultural identity.

Colombia is the third largest producer of coffee in the world, behind Brazil and Vietnam, supplying about 7% of the world’s beans, according to the US Department of Agriculture.

It is known for its distinct, rich and high quality Arabica coffee, grown in volcanic soil in high-altitude microclimates in the Andes.

Monday’s powerful earthquake in Colombia bears remnants of another tragedy which struck the same region more than 25 years ago.

On January 25, 1999, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake hit Colombia’s coffee growing region, leaving 1,185 people dead and more than 8,500 injured, and destroying 35,972 homes, according to data from Colombia’s National Administrative Department of Statistics (DANE).

Most of the deaths (about 921) and damage occurred in the city of Armenia, in western Colombia’s mountainous coffee-growing region, which has also been one of the hardest hit by today’s quake.

“I was very young, but I remember that tragedy too. And now it’s happening again in that same Coffee Axis region—in Pereira and Manizales. I don’t even want to think about what those people are going through. It’s all very sad,” Carlos Atuesta, a professor at the National University, told CNN.

The 1999 tragedy prompted Colombia to better prepare itself for major earthquakes; now, evacuation drills are conducted at least twice a year in cities such as Bogotá, Medellín, Baranquilla and Cali.

The US State Department is “actively assisting” Americans affected by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake in Colombia, according to an X post from the US embassy in Bogotá.

Hundreds of thousands of Americans visit Colombia every year, forming the largest share of tourists to the country.

At least 132 people have died, and 570 have been injured as a result of the earthquake that struck early Monday in western Colombia, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities.

Emergency responders are racing to dig people out of the rubble. Among the collapsed structures were the pediatric and neonatal sections of a hospital in Cali, and the government has declared a national disaster and deployed soldiers to the area.

Scroll through for photos of the scene in Colombia after the earthquake:

Sixteen people were rescued from an aerial cable car system in the western Colombian city of Pereira, the city’s mayor’s office said Monday.

The passengers were inside the cable car cabins when the powerful earthquake struck Monday morning and were successfully evacuated roughly six hours later, around 1:30 p.m. local time, the statement said.

Service on Pereira’s cable car system will remain suspended until further notice while safety inspections are conducted, the statement said.

Aerial cable cars are a popular form of public transit in Colombia, connecting commuters in hillside communities with city centers.

Manizales, another city in Colombia’s mountainous coffee region, also had to evacuate passengers and suspend service on its cable car system due to structural damage, the city’s mayor said earlier.

At least 132 people have died, and 570 have been injured as a result of the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck earlier Monday, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, which earlier took part in an disaster response meeting with the president.

The city of Pereira has reported 60 deaths alone, the association said.

Five capital cities across the country are in a red alert, 86 buildings have collapsed and seven airports have suspended operations, the association added.

Colombian singer Karol G said on social media Monday that her foundation Con Cora is working to address the emergency in the country and “find the best way to support affected families” after the 7.4 magnitude earthquake.

“My solidarity, my heart, and my prayers are with all the people affected by the earthquake in Colombia and with so many families who are going through moments of pain and uncertainty today,” she wrote in an Instagram story.

Karol G is among several Colombian artists and celebrities who have expressed solidarity with those affected.

Earlier, Shakira offered a message of support, saying, “My heart is with everyone who felt this earthquake today and with the families who are going through moments of anguish.”

The United States is committing $15.5 million in funding to Colombia for shelter, food, protection and earthquake assessments after a magnitude 7.4 quake struck the country today, the State Department announced Monday on X.

“We are united in prayer with the Colombian people and stand ready to support President (Abelardo de la Espriella) and his government as they assess the needs on the ground,” the State Department said in a statement.

The 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia occurred just over a month after two quakes killed more than 6,300 people in neighboring Venezuela. Other than sharing the same tectonic plate, however, the tremors don’t have much in common, according to a geology expert.

“The geological and geotectonic context is completely different,” said Gustavo Ortiz, a PhD in geological sciences from Argentina’s National Scientific and Technical Research Council.

In western South America, quakes often strike when one plate — in this case the Nazca Plate in the Pacific — sinks beneath the South American Plate, in a process known as subduction, Ortiz told CNN’s Rafael Romo.

“In contrast, for that fateful earthquake in Venezuela, the plates interacting were the South American and Caribbean plates, further north. In that instance, the plates moved laterally against each other, and no subduction occurred,” he said.

Ortiz noted the earthquakes in Venezuela occurred near the surface — at a depth of less than 20 kilometers (about 12.5 miles) — whereas the seismic event recorded earlier this Monday in Colombia took place at a depth of more than 100 kilometers ( about 62 miles).

When the shaking started, I was on my way to my son’s school in southern Cali for an 8 a.m. appointment. My car began moving in a very strange way, and it wasn’t until we saw utility poles swaying that we realized an earthquake was happening.

When I arrived at the school, the appointment had been cancelled because they were busy assessing damage. On the drive back home to southwestern Cali, we encountered areas without power and traffic lights that weren’t working.

An hour after the quake, many people were still being evacuated from their buildings, unable to re-enter because of the damage.

Some of the damage was concentrated in the area near the bullring (Plaza de Toros), where buildings have collapsed facades and cracks and one building has completely collapsed.

Communication networks failed. Calls wouldn’t go through, and mobile data wasn’t working either. Because of this, businesses like gas stations were only accepting cash. By midday, many supermarkets still hadn’t opened.

At my home, books fell off the shelves and drawers slid open. There is a large crack in my apartment block, and many roof tiles are on the verge of falling.

I have received reports from acquaintances whose apartment is no longer habitable due to cracks and the risk of imminent collapse. Reports keep coming in from people across the city: commercial buildings that have collapsed and street corners in southern Cali that have been devastated.

It is usually very hot in Cali, but today is exceptionally hot.

At 7 a.m. there wasn’t a single cloud in the sky, and it has remained largely clear since then. Right now, the temperature is 33°C (91°F), with a “feels-like” temperature of 34°C (93°F).

World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés says his disaster-relief network has been “activated” to deploy emergency food aid to Colombia following today’s earthquake.

“Let’s hope for the best… ” Andrés said in a post on social media.

The chef-led relief organization often sets up outdoor kitchens in disaster areas and war zones, distributing free meals. The charity has served people in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon and Ukraine, and last month was active in Venezuela after the devastating pair of earthquakes there.

Juan Camilo Jiménez, the organization’s response director for Colombia, told CNN that WCK already has local networks on the ground there.

“The plan is we work with local resources, local restaurants that have been cooking before the earthquake,” said Camilo. “We partner with them and pay for meals that we are going to be providing. In that way, we help those restaurants that are probably going to struggle in the next few days.”

The main challenge in earthquake-affected areas are finding safe spaces to work that can withstand any earthquake aftershocks, Camilo said. The next is refrigeration for ingredients. He added that WCK does not set a deadline or target number of meals they want to provide, preferring to assess the situation on the ground first.

“We arrive and we like to understand the situation firsthand, then we’re going to find the scope of the response,” said Camilo.

Colombian Vice President José Manuel Restrepo announced he is heading to Manizales to lead the Unified Command Post, from where he will coordinate the response to the earthquake.

“This difficult moment we are facing requires solidarity and action,” Restrepo said in a message posted on social media.

Manizales, located in the department of Caldas, is one of the areas hardest hit by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday.

The vice president also stated he would work with the Foreign Ministry to arrange for the arrival of resources and support from the international community.

The epicenter of Monday’s earthquake was in Chocó, Colombia’s poorest department, where more than two-thirds of the population live in poverty, according to government statistics.

Apart from Quibdo, the capital, much of the region is accessible only by air or water because it has few roads, according to a 2021 report by ACAPS. In recent years, the region has also struggled with violence from organized crime groups and militant organizations, including the National Liberation Army (ELN).

Outside of Chocó, the quake also shook part of the country’s “Coffee Axis,” a hub for the prodigious Colombian coffee business. Dozens of people have died in Riselralda, a department in the heart of the Coffee Axis, and cities throughout the region have reported extensive damage.

Several patients are trapped under the rubble of a partially collapsed hospital in Cali, western Colombia, according to a local official.

Some sections of the Cali’s University Hospital, including the pediatrics department, “have collapsed,” the governor of Valle del Cauca, Dilian Francisca Toro, told local media.

“Consequently, there are people trapped,” she said in a video posted to X. Firefighters and the army are “working to get them”.

About 30% of the hospital’s infrastructure has collapsed, including three floors reserved for pediatrics, internal medicine and part of the neonatal unit, the manager Irne Torres Castro told reporters.

At least four people have been rescued from under the rubble, according to the government of Cali. Many patients were evacuated and treated outside at the hospital’s gardens. Some were taken to other health facilities.

The hospital is among several health institutions in Cali that have been closed and evacuated because of structural damage, the local government said.

Paramedics could be seen wheeling people out on gurneys as medical workers circled the hospital courtyard, in social media footage.

We’re continuing to track developments after a powerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia earlier today.

At least 111 people have died, according to Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella. The government has declared a state of national disaster, and soldiers are being deployed to affected areas of the country.

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in the northwestern department of Chocó, about 240 kilometers (or 150 miles) west of Bogotá.

If you’re just joining us, catch up on the latest:

CNN’s Michael Rios, Gonzalo Zegarra, Max Saltman, Juan Carlos Paz, Sana Noor Haq, Sol Amaya and Elise Hammond contributed to this report.

The strongest earthquake to hit Colombia in the last decade shook the South American country on Monday, killing dozens of people, pancaking buildings to the ground and catapulting communities into a state of national disaster.

With the death toll steadily climbing following the 7.4 magnitude quake, emergency crews are racing to try and recover survivors trapped beneath the rubble.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella – who only took office on Friday – called an emergency committee to “personally lead efforts” to try and rescue people trapped in the wreckage.

Further afield, international leaders in the US, South America, Europe and the Middle East have also pledged to support ongoing rescue operations.
